html:
The Savitsky Museum in Nukus, capital of Karakalpakstan in western Uzbekistan, holds one of the world's largest collections of Russian avant-garde art. It opened in 1966.

Its founder, the painter and archaeologist Igor Savitsky, came to the region to work on digs in ancient Khwarazm and to collect Karakalpak folk art: jewellery, textiles and yurt hangings. He then began buying works by artists whose modernist styles had been banned in favour of Socialist Realism, many of them dead or sent to the camps. He bought from widows and families and hid the paintings far from Moscow.

Because Nukus was so remote, the censors left it alone. By his death in 1984 Savitsky had gathered tens of thousands of objects; the museum now holds over 82,000. It is often called the "Louvre of the desert", and stands near the dying Aral Sea.
sum: The Savitsky Museum in Nukus, capital of Karakalpakstan in western Uzbekistan, holds one of the world's largest collections of Russian avant-garde art. It opened in 1966.
